steps.title: Text A · Four rules, no reasons
steps.html:
Written for this course.

Every organisation has at least one rule that nobody on the staff can account for. A German manufacturer insists on drivers reversing into every space in the car park. A firm in Osaka does not allow anybody to leave the building during the lunch break. A London agency once told its people that personal calls made at a desk would count against them at the annual review. A Rotterdam warehouse requires two signatures on a form that only one person ever reads. None of the four ever explained why, and in three of them the rule still applies to visitors as well as to employees.

The Osaka rule resists the obvious explanation. It can’t have been about laziness, since the same staff regularly work late without being asked twice. It might have been about the telephones, which somebody has to answer at one o’clock, or it could have been a way of protecting the younger employees from being sent out on errands during the only hour that belongs to them. Both readings fit the evidence; neither can be confirmed, and the company has never justified the working practice in writing.

The London rule is the easiest to reconstruct and the least flattering. Somebody must have complained about one particular colleague. The agency can’t have wanted to accuse that person openly, because a direct conversation would have identified the complainant as well. Writing a rule that applies to everybody was simpler than choosing to criticize one person for it, and it allowed the management to blame nobody in public while making the point in private. It may not have been fair, but it worked, and nobody in the office could have proved who it was aimed at.

steps.title: Text B · Reading a rule backwards
steps.html:
Written for this course. Parking guidance from the UK Health and Safety Executive, Workplace Transport Safety.

Turn a rule round and it becomes readable. The German parking rule must have begun as a safety measure rather than a matter of neatness. Britain’s Health and Safety Executive advises that where a site cannot be laid out for drive-through parking, the arrangements should encourage reverse parking, precisely because reversing out into a flow of moving traffic is where the collisions happen. Somebody at that plant may well have read the same guidance. The rule can’t have been invented to make the yard look tidy: a company that only wanted tidiness would not have troubled to enforce it on visitors.

The legal background makes the reasoning tighter. An employer who exposes staff to a risk that could reasonably have been designed out can face harsh penalties, and where the failure is serious enough a manager may be given a suspended sentence rather than a fine. Read in that light, a rule that looks petty starts to look expensive. Nobody wrote it in order to irritate the workforce; somebody wrote it with a lawyer in the room, and the lawyer must have been thinking about what a court would say afterwards.

What unexplained rules have in common is that each one is an answer to a question nobody wrote down. Regulations at work are the residue of incidents, and the incident is almost never recorded beside the regulation it produced. You can’t count on the reason surviving; you can only reconstruct it from the shape of what is left, the way an archaeologist reconstructs a building from the holes its posts left in the ground. The reconstruction is worth doing, because the alternative — assuming that the rule must have been designed to annoy you — is usually wrong, and it is always the least interesting explanation available. Whoever wrote the rule could have added one sentence of explanation, and must have decided, for reasons of their own, not to.

The reconstruction is worth doing, because the alternative — assuming that the rule must have been designed to annoy you — is usually wrong, and it is always the least interesting explanation available. Whoever wrote the rule could have added one sentence of explanation, and must have decided, for reasons of their own, not to.

steps.title: Saying how sure you are about the past
steps.html:
The complete rule, then a large example bank, then a worked transformation.

When you work backwards from evidence, English marks how certain you are with a modal, not with an adverb. The structure is always the same: modal + have + past participle.

Must have = I am sure it happened. Can't have / couldn't have = I am sure it did not happen. Between them sit might have, may have and could have = it is possible.

The opposite of must have is can't have, not mustn't have. Mustn't is a prohibition and is not used for deduction.

For a state rather than an action, add been: It must have been a safety measure. For an ongoing action, use been + -ing: They must have been testing something.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences, all built on the two texts.

It must have been a safety measure.
Sure — the evidence points one way only.

They can't have banned the lunch break.
Sure it did not happen: it would be illegal.

They may have needed someone at the phones.
Possible, no more.

It might have been simple sense in that climate.
Possible; might and may are interchangeable here.

Somebody must have spilt something expensive.
An overnight ban is strong evidence.

She might have expected the criticism.
Possible.

She can't have expected it to travel so fast.
Sure it did not happen.

Somebody must have photographed the list.
It exists in public, so it was photographed.

They can't have done it by accident.
The negative deduction, not mustn't have done.

He could have resigned rather than been fired.
Could have = one possibility among several.

They must have been testing a new policy.
A past action still in progress at that time.

Nobody can have read the whole list in that time.
Can have appears in negatives and questions.

steps.title: Turning evidence into a deduction
steps.html:
1. The evidence: on Monday every desk in the building had a drink on it. On Tuesday drinks were banned everywhere.
  2. Decide how sure you are. A total ban overnight is strong evidence of a single incident, so this is certainty.
  3. Choose the modal: certainty about the past → must have.
  4. Build it: must + have + past participle. The action is spill, whose participle is spilt (or spilled): Somebody must have spilt something.
  5. Now test the opposite. Could a cleaner have asked for it? That is only possible, not certain, so: A cleaner might have asked for it. And what you are sure did not happen: They can't have decided it that morning — never mustn't have decided.

steps.title: Write your explanation.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Describe the rule, then give one deduction you are sure about, one you think is possible, and one thing you are sure is not the reason.
steps.html:
• Describe the rule and say that it was never explained.
  • Give the deduction you are most confident about, with <i>must have</i>.
  • Give a second, weaker possibility, with <i>might / may / could have</i>.
  • Rule one explanation out, with <i>can't have</i>, and say why.

Useful language

  • Nobody was ever told why …
  • It must have been … / They must have decided …
  • It might / may / could have been …
  • They can't have … , because …
  • The obvious explanation would be … , but that doesn't fit.
  • Whatever the reason, staff were never told.
steps.modelHtml:
The lift that stops at every floor

The lift in my first office was set to stop at every floor on the way down, whether or not anybody had called it. Nobody was ever told why, and the sign on the wall said only that the setting was permanent.

It must have been a decision taken after something went wrong, because the setting was changed overnight, and the maintenance company was in the building that week. It might also have been about the ground-floor security desk: stopping at every floor meant everyone passed the camera on level one.

What it can't have been is energy saving. The lift used more power, not less, and the building manager was criticized for the bills all year.

Three years later nobody has explained it, and the setting is still there.
